tools.name: time_now
tools.description: Returns the authoritative current time in one or more timezones, with UTC offset, ISO week number, day of year, weekend flag, and daylight-saving state. Use this instead of guessing the date: a language model has no clock, and its training cutoff is not today.

tools.name: time_convert
tools.description: Converts one instant into any number of timezones, handling daylight saving transitions correctly. Naive inputs (no Z or offset) are read as wall-clock time in `from`; inputs carrying an offset are absolute.

tools.name: time_diff
tools.description: Computes the elapsed time between two instants: exact totals in each unit, a calendar breakdown (years/months/days rather than 'thirteen and a half months'), the count of weekdays in between, and a human phrase. Negative when `to` precedes `from`.

tools.name: time_window
tools.description: Answers the questions a deadline actually poses: is this instant inside the window, how long until it opens or closes, and if it is outside, by how much. tools.name: cron_next
tools.description: Parses a standard 5-field cron expression (or 6-field with leading seconds, or a macro like @daily), validates it, describes it in plain English, and computes the next run times in a given timezone with daylight-saving handled. tools.name: json_query
tools.description: Runs a JSONPath query and returns the matching values with their concrete paths. Supports property access, array indexing (including negative indices), slices, wildcards, recursive descent (`..`) and filters (`[?(@.price > 10)]`). tools.name: json_repair
tools.description: Takes JSON that almost parses and makes it parse: markdown code fences, prose wrapped around the object, trailing commas, single or smart quotes, unquoted keys, Python True/False/None, comments, NaN, and brackets left open by a truncated response. tools.name: hash
tools.description: Computes cryptographic digests and HMAC signatures. Returns hex and base64 at once, so a webhook signature can be compared in whichever encoding the provider uses. MD5 and CRC32 are included for checksums and legacy fixtures; they are not secure for authentication.

tools.name: math_eval
tools.description: Evaluates arithmetic with correct operator precedence, parentheses, exponentiation, factorials, named variables and 30+ functions. Language models perform arithmetic by pattern-matching and quietly get long multiplications and compounding wrong; this computes the number instead of predicting it.

tools.name: http_check
tools.description: Resolves a URL and reports what actually happens to it — final status, the full redirect chain, content type and page title. tools.name: http_assert
tools.description: The difference between an agent believing it succeeded and knowing it did. http.check tells you a URL is alive; this tells you it is correct. tools.description: Searches every tool by name, summary, description and keywords, and returns the closest matches with their endpoints and parameters. findings.title: Lethal trifecta: untrusted input + private data + external sink
findings.detail: Server "mcp" exposes tools that together enable an exfiltration flow. Untrusted content: json_repair, http_check, http_assert · Private data: json_query, edi_parse, edi_validate, edi_build · Public sink: hash · Destructive: cron_next, math_eval.

evidence.snippet: Untrusted content: json_repair, http_check, http_assert · Private data: json_query, edi_parse, edi_validate, edi_build · Public sink: hash · Destructive: cron_next, math_eval

findings.remediation: Do not co-install these capabilities under one trust boundary; an injected comment/email can steer the model to exfiltrate via the sink tool.
